claims.text: The starting alloy has composition Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
The alloy is produced as a melt-spun ribbon at a cooling rate of at least 10^5 K/s in an inert atmosphere.
The rapidly quenched ribbon exhibits prevalent surface oxidation.
Surface oxidation and other surface nucleation sites lead to primary crystalline-phase formation in this alloy.
The proposed intervention is immediate PVD deposition of a uniform, approximately 50 nm SiO2 coating after rapid quenching.
A SiO2 coating will suppress surface-induced heterogeneous nucleation.
The SiO2 barrier reduces or passivates surface defects and oxidation sites that act as heterogeneous nucleation centers.
Passivation by SiO2 obstructs the formation of surface nucleation sites that would otherwise trigger extensive primary crystallization.
The SiO2 barrier minimizes atomic rearrangements that lead to crystallization.
A coating deposited after quenching stabilizes the amorphous structure during rapid cooling.
The coating stabilizes the amorphous structure during subsequent moderate reheating.
Coated specimens will retain a higher amorphous volume fraction than identically processed uncoated specimens.
Coated specimens will exhibit a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than uncoated specimens.
Cooling rates of at least 10^5 K/s and reheating between 0.8Tg and Tg are the relevant operating boundaries for the proposed effect.
The intervention's success depends critically on obtaining a uniform and adherent SiO2 coating.
A nonuniform or poorly adherent coating may incompletely suppress surface nucleation and reduce improvements in amorphous retention and thermal stability.

contradictions.description: The coating is deposited only after rapid quenching, but the mechanism claims that it suppresses crystallization during that already-completed rapid-cooling step. It can directly affect subsequent reheating, not prior solidification.

Reheating is restricted to 0.8Tg–Tg, yet crystallization-onset temperature and crystallization exotherms are designated as primary DSC outcomes. A scan terminating at Tg may not reach the crystallization onset, especially if the intervention shifts that onset upward.

The uncertainty field treats a nonuniform or poorly adherent coating as an implementation failure that can mask the effect, whereas the falsification rule treats poor coating quality itself as refutation of the surface-passivation hypothesis.
